header: Stereo. H C J D A 38.
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT LAHORE
body: Date of hearing 11.11.2026 Applicant by Syed Zain-ul-Abidein Bokhari, Advocate Respondent by: Mr. Ghulam Akbar Khosa, Advocate.

Muhammad Ajmal Zahid, J.— Through this consolidated judgment, we intend to decide the instant Sales Tax Reference Application along with connected STR Nos.40131/2022, 40132/2022, and7 40134/2022, filed under Section 47 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 (“the Act”), whereby the applicant-department has called into question the legality of the order dated 15.03.2022 passed by the learned Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Division Bench-1, Islamabad (“the learned Tribunal”), in STA Nos.202/IB/2021, 203/IB/2021, 204/IB/2021 and 205/IB/2021.

2. Briefly stated, the facts giving rise to the instant Reference Application along with the connected Reference Applications are that the department, on the basis of information received through reports from the Directorate of Intelligence and Investigation, Faisalabad, alleged that the respondent-registered person, M/s Azhar Corporation (Pvt.) Ltd., engaged in the manufacture of ghee and cooking oil, had made supplies of ghee and cooking oil to registered/unregistered persons during the tax periods falling within July 2015 to June 2019, corresponding to Tax Years 2016 to 2019, respectively. The declared value of such supplies was determined as Rs.15,726,738/- for Tax Year 2016, Rs.14,620,086/- STR No.40130/2022 2 for Tax Year 2017, Rs.16,472,068/- for Tax Year 2018 and Rs.12,852,012/- for Tax Year 2019. The department alleged that the said supplies attracted sales tax at the rate of 17% under Section 3 read with Serial No.24 of the Sixth Schedule to the Act. Upon examination of the relevant record and audit proceedings, certain discrepancies were allegedly noticed, whereupon Show- Cause Notices bearing Nos.2497, 2498 and 2499, all dated 21.12.2020, and No.2501 dated 22.12.2020, were issued to the respondent-registered person. The explanations furnished by the respondent-registered person were not found satisfactory by the adjudicating authority, which consequently determined sales tax liabilities of Rs.2,673,545/-, Rs.2,485,415/-, Rs.2,800,252/- and Rs.2,184,012/- for Tax Years 2016, 2017, 2018 and 2019, respectively, along with further tax of Rs.314,535/-, Rs.292,402/-, Rs.329,441/- and Rs.385,560/-, respectively, besides default surcharge under Section 34 and penalties amounting to Rs.138,891/-, Rs.138,891/-, Rs.156,584/- and Rs.128,520/-, respectively, under Section 33(5) of the Act.

3. The respondent-registered person, being aggrieved by the orders passed by the adjudicating authorities, approached the learned Tribunal through the aforementioned appeals. The learned Tribunal, vide orders dated 15.03.2022 passed in all the aforementioned STAs, accepted the appeals of the respondentregistered person and set aside the impugned orders, principally on the ground that the department could not lawfully determine and recover sales tax liability for a period preceding the date of actual or compulsory registration of the respondent-registered person. The applicant-department, feeling aggrieved, has invoked the reference jurisdiction of this Court through the instant and connected Reference Applications.

4. Learned counsel for the applicant-department contends that the learned Tribunal has misconstrued the provisions of the Act, particularly Sections 2(25) and 3 thereof, while holding that a STR No.40130/2022 3 person who has not actually been registered under the Act cannot be subjected to sales tax liability for the period during which he was otherwise legally required to obtain registration. He submits that the definition of "registered person" contained in Section 2(25) expressly encompasses not only a person, who has actually been registered, but also a person who is liable to be registered under the Act. Adds that both categories have been deliberately brought within the statutory definition, and the respondentregistered person cannot escape its fiscal obligations merely by failing to obtain registration despite being legally obliged to do so. He further submits that Section 3(1) of the Act is the charging provision and imposes sales tax upon taxable supplies made by a registered person in the course or furtherance of any taxable activity. Since the definition of registered person under Section 2(25) includes a person liable to be registered, the liability to pay sales tax arises from the date on which such person becomes liable to obtain registration and not merely from the date on which the department subsequently completes the process of compulsory registration. Learned counsel further argues that Rule 6(4) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 (“the Rules”) cannot be interpreted so as to override or restrict the charging provision contained in Section 3 of the Act. He submits that the Rules have been framed in exercise of the rule-making power conferred by Section 50 of the Act and must remain subordinate to the substantive provisions of the statute. Further adds that Rule 6(4) of the Rules merely prescribes the procedure and manner in which a person is to be compulsorily registered and cannot be construed as granting immunity from the tax liability which has already arisen under the parent statute. He also contends that the respondent-registered person was engaged in making taxable supplies and was, therefore, under a statutory obligation to obtain registration. Adds that the absence of a Sales Tax Registration Number, PIN code or password cannot be converted into a defence against the department when the STR No.40130/2022 4 respondent-registered person itself was responsible for not obtaining registration within the prescribed period. He maintains that the inability of an unregistered person to issue a tax invoice or to furnish an electronic return cannot defeat the charging provision or confer upon such person an advantage arising from his own failure to comply with the law. Learned counsel lastly submits that the learned Tribunal has failed to appreciate the judgment rendered by this Court in Commissioner Inland Revenue, Gujranwala v. S.K. Steel Casting, Gujranwala (2019 PTD 1493), in its proper perspective, the judgement was upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan by way of leave refusing order dated 11.03.2020 in Civil Petitions No.2117-L to 2122-L, 2153-1 to 2159-L, 2211-L to 2214-L, 2450-L to 2453-L & 2471-L of 2019. He argues that the impugned order is contrary to the statutory scheme and the principles enunciated in the aforesaid judgment. He, therefore, prays that the impugned order of the learned Tribunal be set aside.

5. Conversely, learned counsel for the respondent-registered person supports the impugned order and submits that the learned Tribunal has correctly interpreted the relevant provisions of the Act and the Rules. He contends that the department could not lawfully create sales tax liability for the period preceding the actual or compulsory registration of the respondent-registered person, particularly when the statutory procedure prescribed under Rule 6 of the Rules had not been followed. He submits that the definition contained in Section 2(25) of the Act cannot be read in isolation or applied mechanically without considering the nature, scope and mechanism of the charging and procedural provisions of the Act. He further maintains that the statutory framework contemplates a registered person who is capable of issuing a tax invoice, collecting output tax, claiming admissible input tax and furnishing electronic-returns in the prescribed manner. An unregistered person, having no registration number or access to the STR No.40130/2022 5 prescribed electronic mechanism, cannot be expected to discharge obligations which the statute itself attaches to a registered person. He accordingly prays for dismissal of the Reference Applications.
6. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and have examined the available record.

7. The controversy involved in these Reference Applications revolves around the interpretation and application of Sections 2(24), 2(25), 2(37), 3, 6, 7, 8, 8B, 11, 14, 22, 23, 25, 33, 34 and 38 of the Act, read with Rule 6 of the Rules. The principal questions requiring determination by this Court are as follows: i. Whether the expression "registered person", as defined under Section 2(25) of the Act, includes a person who is merely liable to be registered but has not actually been registered, for the purposes of imposing and recovering sales tax under Section 3 of the Act?

ii. Whether the department can determine and recover sales tax liability for a period preceding the date of actual or compulsory registration by relying upon the extended definition of "registered person"
contained in Section 2(25) of the Act?

iii. Whether Rule 6(4) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006, which requires a person compulsorily registered to comply with the provisions of the Act and the Rules from the date of compulsory registration, can be disregarded while determining liability under the charging provision?

iv. Whether the omission of the former Section 19 of the Act and the subsequent statutory framework governing compulsory registration have any bearing upon the interpretation of the liability of a person who was liable to be registered but remained unregistered?
v. Whether the judgment of this Court in S.K. Steel Casting (supra) supports the case of the applicantdepartment or, rather, governs the controversy against it?

8. Before proceeding to examine the rival contentions, it would be appropriate to appreciate the nature of sales tax and the STR No.40130/2022 6 statutory mechanism devised by the legislature under the Act. Sales tax is an indirect tax ordinarily imposed upon the taxable supply or import of goods, the ultimate economic burden whereof is intended to be borne by the end consumer. The registered person, in the statutory chain of transactions, performs the function of collecting and depositing tax in accordance with the mechanism prescribed by law. The Act, therefore, does not merely provide for the imposition of a tax on a taxable transaction; rather, it establishes an integrated mechanism for registration, collection, adjustment, payment, reporting and recovery of tax.

9. The statutory scheme is essentially based upon the valueadded tax mechanism, commonly known as the VAT system. Under this mechanism, a registered person making taxable supplies charges output tax, while being entitled, subject to the restrictions imposed by the Act, to claim adjustment of admissible input tax paid on purchases or acquisitions. The difference between output tax and admissible input tax constitutes the net tax payable for the relevant tax period. Consequently, the charging provision cannot be examined in isolation from the provisions governing registration, issuance of tax invoices, maintenance of records, adjustment of input tax and filing of electronic returns. The provisions of the Act must be construed together so that each provision is given its due effect without rendering another provision redundant or irrelevant which is edict of statute. Reliance is placed on Commissioner Inland Revenue Regional Tax Office, Peshawar v. Messrs Cherat Cement Company Ltd. Nowshera (2026 SCMR 545), The Commissioner Inland Revenue, Legal Zone, Large Taxpayers office, Lahore and another v. Messrs Mayfair Spinning Mills Ltd. And others (2025 SCMR 1), The Commissioner, Inland Revenue, Karachi v. Messrs Attock Cement Pakistan Limited, Karachi (2023 SCMR 279) and Commissioner Inland Revenue Zone-IV, Large Taxpayer Unit, Karachi v. Messrs STR No.40130/2022 7 Al-Abid Silk Mills Ltd., A-39, Manghopir Road, Site, Karachi (2023 SCMR 1797).

10. The principle that a fiscal statute must be construed according to its language, while considering the statute as a whole, is well settled. A taxing liability cannot be imposed merely on the basis of an assumed legislative intention or by extending the scope of a charging provision beyond its express language. Equally, a taxpayer cannot claim exemption from a liability which the statute clearly imposes. The exercise, therefore, is not to favour either the taxpayer or the revenue department, but to ascertain the true legislative intention from the language, context and structure of the enactment. In this regard, guidance may be drawn from Chairman, Federal Board of Revenue v. M/s. Al-Technique Corporation of Pakistan Ltd. (PLD 2017 SC 99), wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan reiterated the settled principles governing the construction of fiscal legislation and the necessity of finding the authority to impose a tax within the express provisions of law.

11. The controversy principally emanates from the interpretation of Sections 2(24) and 2(25) of the Act, which defines the expression “registration number” and "registered person" in the following terms:
(24) "registration number" means the number allocated to the registered person for the purpose of this Act;

(25) "registered person" means a person who is registered or is liable to be registered under this Act: Provided that a person liable to be registered but not registered under this Act 2[] shall not be entitled to any benefit available to a registered person under any of the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder;;

A plain reading of the aforesaid provisions reveals that the expression “registered person” has been given an extended STR No.40130/2022 8 statutory meaning and encompasses two distinct categories of persons. The first category comprises persons who have formally obtained registration under the Act and have consequently been allocated a registration number in accordance with the prescribed procedure. The second category, however, comprises persons who, notwithstanding the absence of formal registration, fall within the statutory parameters of persons liable to be registered under the Act. Thus, the legislature has consciously distinguished between the factual status of being registered and the legal obligation to obtain registration, while bringing both categories within the ambit of the expression “registered person” for the purposes of the Act. Furthermore, Section 2(24), which defines the expression “registration number”, must be read harmoniously with Section 2(25). The former contemplates the allocation of a registration number to a person upon registration, whereas the latter extends the expression “registered person” to include even those persons who are legally liable to obtain registration but have not yet done so. Therefore, collective reading of the aforesaid provisions establishes that the mere liability to obtain registration does not confer upon a person the status of a duly registered person under the Act, unless such person has actually obtained registration and has been allocated a registration number in accordance with the prescribed procedure.

12. The learned Tribunal, while deciding the issue in hand also framed the following questions while dealing with the definition of “registered person” which also reproduced hereunder: i. Whether the charge, levy and pay the tax under section 3 of the Act is on the registered person who is actually registered under the Act or the person who is liable to be registered or both?

ii. Whether the provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder would come into play from the date of voluntary registration or compulsory registration of a person making taxable supplies under the Act?
STR No.40130/2022 9 iii. Whether the Commissioner Inland Revenue (CIR)
has the power to compulsory register a person under section 14 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 6 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 from the date he became liable for registration?

The applicant-department places reliance upon the second limb of the definition and argued that once a person becomes liable to be registered, he automatically assumes the status of a registered person for all purposes of the Act, including the imposition and recovery of sales tax under Section 3 of the Act. Such an interpretation, however, does not take into account the qualifying language with which Section 2 commences, i.e., "unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context…..".

13. The opening words of Section 2 are of considerable significance. They demonstrate that the definitions contained therein are not to be applied mechanically or divorced from the context in which a particular expression occurs. A definition clause ordinarily supplies the meaning of an expression wherever it appears in the statute; however, where the application of the defined expression to a particular provision produces a result inconsistent with the language, context or scheme of that provision, the definition must yield to the contextual requirement.

14. In Syed Muhammad Haider Zaidi and others v. Abdul Hafeez and others (1991 SCMR 1699), the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan recognized the principle that a definition contained in the interpretation clause is required to be read in the context of the provision in which the defined expression is employed. It cannot be applied in a manner which defeats the legislative scheme or produces an interpretation inconsistent with the subject and context of the enactment. The definition clauses are not absolute as they are directory in nature and are qualified by context and subject. Reliance in this regard is placed on Rafhan Maize Products Co. Ltd. v. The Commissioner of Income-Tax STR No.40130/2022 10 (1988 PTD 571), M/s Khawaja Auto Cars Ltd. v. Muhammad Yousaf, (1991 SCMR 2223).

15. In interpreting a definition clause, the language employed by the legislature must be read in the context of the enactment as a whole and in accordance with its object and scheme. In Commissioner of Income Tax v. Khurshid Ahmad (PLD 2016 SC 545) and Al-Technique Corporation (supra), the Hon’ble Supreme Court emphasized the importance of construing statutory language in its proper legislative context. The same interpretative approach is reflected in "Pakistan Stock Exchange v. CIR (2026 SCMR 373), Pakistan Match Industries (Pvt.) Ltd. and others v. Assistant Collector, Sales Tax and Central Excise, Mardan and others (2019 SCMR 906), Aurangzaib v. Medipak (Pvt.) Ltd. and others (2018 SCMR 2027), Muhammad Hanif Abbasi v. Imran Khan Niazi and others (PLD 2018 SC 189), Syed Mushahid Shah and others v. Federal Investigation Agency and others (2017 SCMR 1218), Commissioner of Income Tax v. Khurshid Ahmad (PLD 2016 SC 545), Muhammad Khan v. Obaidullah Jan Babat and others (PLD 2016 SC 492). The governing principle is that the statutory definition must be applied in a manner that gives effect to the language chosen by the legislature without unduly enlarging or restricting its scope.

16. It is, therefore, necessary to distinguish between the legal obligation to obtain registration and the consequences which follow upon actual registration. The expression "liable to be registered" identifies a person who has incurred a statutory obligation to seek registration. It does not necessarily follow that such person, merely by incurring that obligation, becomes capable of performing every act which the statute expressly requires to be performed by a registered person. The distinction assumes particular significance when the definition is read alongside Sections 3, 6, 7, 22, 23 and 26 of the Act. These provisions collectively contemplate a statutory framework in which STR No.40130/2022 11 registration is not a mere formality but an essential component of the mechanism for the collection, adjustment and payment of sales tax. We are, therefore, unable to subscribe to the proposition that the second limb of Section 2(25) along with section 2(24), without regard to the remaining provisions of the Act, can be employed as an independent source for creating and enforcing a tax demand for every period preceding compulsory registration.

17. Section 3 of the Act constitutes the charging provision and provides for the levy and collection of sales tax upon taxable supplies made by a registered person in the course or furtherance of any taxable activity carried on by him, as well as upon goods imported into Pakistan, subject to the provisions of the Act. The words "subject to the provisions of this Act" are of particular relevance. They indicate that the charge under Section 3 is not to be administered in disregard of the other provisions governing the statutory liability and the manner of its determination and discharge.

18. The applicant-department is correct to the extent that Section 2(25) includes a person liable to be registered within the extended definition of a registered person. However, the real question is whether that definition can be applied to Section 3 in such a manner as to dispense with the registration procedure prescribed by the Act and the Rules. In our considered view, the answer must be in the negative. Section 3 cannot be read in isolation, nor can the expression "registered person" occurring therein be interpreted without reference to the statutory obligations attached to registration. The charging provision and the machinery provisions must operate harmoniously. The definition cannot be employed to create a liability through a procedure which the legislature has separately prescribed and which has not been followed. There will be harmonious construction of statutes as a whole Reliance in this regard is placed on The Province of Punjab through Chief Secretary, Government of the Punjab, Lahore and STR No.40130/2022 12 others v. T & T Employees Ideal Cooperative Housing Society Limited (PLD 2026 SC 69), Chairman, National Accountability Bureau through Prosecutor General Accountability, NAB, Islamabad and another v. Adeel Ahmed and others (PLD 2026 SC 424), Raja Amer Khan and others v. Federation of Pakistan through Secfretary, Law and Justice Division, Ministry of Law and Justice, Islamabad and others (PLD 2025 SC 869), Federation of Pakistan through the Secretary, Ministry of Law and Justice, Islamabad and others v. Supreme Judicial Council through Secretary, Supreme Court Building, Islamabad and others (PLD 2024 SC 698), Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) through Chairman and another v. Messrs ARY Communications Private Limited (ARY Digital) through Chief Executive Officers and another) (PLD 2023 SC 431), Waqar Zafar Bakhiawari and 6 others v. Haji Mazhar Hussain Shah and others (PLD 2018 S.C. 81), Collector of Customs, Customs House, Karachi v. Syed Rehan Ahmad (2017 SCMR 152), Lucky Cement Ltd., v. Commissioner Income Tax, Zone Companies, Circle-5, Peshawar (2015 SCMR 1494), Kamaluddin Qureshi v. Ali International Co. (PLD 2009 SC 367), Mirza Shaukat Baig and others v. Shahid Jamil and others (PLD 2005 SC 530), D.G. Khan Cement Company Ltd. and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others (2004 PTD 1179), Qazi Hussain Ahmad, Ameer Jamaat-e-Islami Pakistan and others v. General Pervez Musharraf, Chief Executive and others (PLD 2002 SC 853), Bashir Ahmad v. Member (Colonies), Board of Revenue, Punjab Lahore and 2 others (PLD 1997 SC 294), Collector of Sales Tax and Central Excise (Enforcement) and another v. Messrs Mega Tech (Pvt.) Ltd. (2005 PTD 1933) , Director, Directorate General of Intelligence and Investigation and others v. Messrs Al-Faiz Industries (Pvt.) Limited and others (2006 SCMR 129), Aftab Shahban Mirani and others v. Muhammad Ibrahim and others (PLD 2008 SC 779), Laylpoor Cotton Mills Ltd. v. The STR No.40130/2022 13 Commissioner, Sargodha Division and another (PLD 1976 SC 615), Salahuddin and 2 others v. Frontier Sugar Mills & Distillery Ltd., Tokht Bhai and 10 others (PLD 1975 SC 244) and Madanlal Fakirchand Dudhediya vs. Shree Changdeo Sugar Mills Limited (AIR 1962 SC 1543).

19. Section 6 of the Act prescribes the time and manner of payment of sales tax. The statutory mechanism requires the registered person to discharge the tax liability arising from taxable supplies in the manner prescribed by law. Section 7, on the other hand, provides for the determination of tax liability by allowing adjustment of admissible input tax against output tax, subject to the restrictions contained in the Act. Section 8 enumerates circumstances in which input tax credit is not allowable, whereas Section 8B provides for restrictions upon adjustment of input tax, subject to the statutory exceptions and conditions. These provisions demonstrate that the legislature has not intended sales tax to operate merely as a tax on the gross value of every supply, divorced from the prescribed mechanism of input and output tax adjustment. The liability of a registered person is determined through a structured process in which the tax charged on supplies and the admissible input tax are reconciled for the relevant tax period.

20. A person who has not been registered is not placed within the ordinary statutory mechanism for claiming input tax adjustment, furnishing electronic returns and discharging net tax liability. To impose upon such person the entire consequences of registration retrospectively, without first following the procedure for compulsory registration, would disregard the statutory sequence contemplated by the Act. It is, however, clarified that this conclusion does not mean that a person who has failed to obtain registration is immune from all consequences arising from such failure. The Act itself provides separate consequences for failure to comply with the obligation to obtain registration under STR No.40130/2022 14 section 33(7) of the Act. The question is whether the department can, without following the prescribed registration procedure, treat the person as having been registered for the purpose of raising a demand under Section 3 for a previous period. That question must be answered with reference to the express provisions of the Act and Rule 6 of the Rules.

21. Section 14 of the Act provides the statutory framework governing registration. It identifies the persons who are required to be registered and casts upon them an obligation to obtain registration in accordance with the prescribed procedure. The obligation to seek registration is, therefore, distinct from the administrative process through which compulsory registration is effected where a person fails to discharge that obligation voluntarily. Section 50 empowers the competent authority to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act. Rules framed in exercise of such statutory authority are not merely administrative instructions; they constitute delegated legislation and are required to be given effect, provided they remain consistent with the parent statute. Rule prescribed under section 50 as statutory force and claim of right on the basis of rule cannot be dispense with as the charge of tax u/s 3 is subject to provision of the Act.
22. In this regard, Rule 6 of the Rules, prescribes the procedure for compulsory registration. For convenience of reference the said Rule is reproduced below:

“6. Compulsory registration:- (1) … (2) … (3) … (4) A person registered compulsorily under sub-rule (2) or (3) is required to comply with all the provisions of the Act and rules made thereunder from the date of compulsory registration, and in case of failure to do so, the Commissioner Inland Revenue having jurisdiction may issue notice under section 25 of the Act for production of records or documents and appearance in person to assess the amount of sales tax payable under section 11 of the STR No.40130/2022 15 Act, and take any other action as required under the law against such person:

Provided that if it is subsequently established that a person was not liable to be registered but was wrongly registered under this rule due to inadvertence, error or misconstruction, the Commissioner shall cause to cancel his registration through the computerized system. In case of such cancellation of registration, such person shall not be liable to pay any tax, default surcharge of penalty under the Act or rules made thereunder, subject to the conditions, limitations and restrictions prescribed under section 3B of the Act.” (emphasis supplied)

The language employed in sub-rule (4) is explicit and leaves little room for ambiguity. It stipulates that a person compulsorily registered under the preceding sub-rules is required to comply with the provisions of the Act and the Rules from the date of compulsory registration.

23. The significance of the expression "from the date of compulsory registration" cannot be overlooked. The legislature, through the delegated legislation, has prescribed a definite point from which the person compulsorily registered is required to comply with the obligations imposed upon a registered person under the Act and the Rules. The department cannot disregard this express statutory prescription while determining liability under the Act.

24. The procedure prescribed under Rule 6 is not an empty formality. It requires the competent authority to undertake an inquiry, issue notice to the person concerned, afford an opportunity to contest his liability to be registered, and thereafter pass an appropriate order. Where the person fails to respond, the Rule provides a separate mechanism for compulsory registration, subject to intimation in the prescribed manner. These requirements are designed to ensure that the question whether a particular person falls within the categories liable to registration is STR No.40130/2022 16 determined through a lawful process rather than being presumed merely on the basis of information available with the department.

25. The proviso to Rule 6(4) further reinforces the importance of the prescribed procedure. It contemplates a situation in which a person is subsequently found not to have been liable to registration but was wrongly registered owing to inadvertence, error or misconstruction. In such circumstances, the Rule provides for cancellation of registration and stipulates the consequences thereof. This safeguard would lose much of its significance if the department were permitted to bypass the procedure and impose liability without first determining the person's status in accordance with the Rule.

26. We are conscious of the settled principle that delegated legislation cannot override, amend or curtail the substantive provisions of the parent statute. However, that principle does not assist the applicant-department in the present controversy. Rule 6(4) does not purport to amend the charging provision or grant an exemption from tax. Rather, it prescribes the procedural and temporal framework within which a person compulsorily registered is required to comply with the statutory obligations attached to registration.

27. The charging provision itself is expressly subject to the provisions of the Act. Therefore, Section 3 and Rule 6 must be construed harmoniously. Where the statute prescribes an obligation to obtain registration and the Rules provide the manner in which compulsory registration is to be effected, the department is required to act in accordance with that statutory mechanism.

28. It is equally important to observe that the power to determine tax liability cannot be exercised independently of the conditions and procedures prescribed by law. Where the law requires a thing to be done in a particular manner, it must be done STR No.40130/2022 17 in that manner or not at all, is relevant in appreciating the mandatory character of the procedure prescribed under Rule 6.

29. The interpretation adopted by us also finds support from the provisions governing maintenance of records, issuance of tax invoices and furnishing of electronic returns. Section 22 of the Act provides for maintenance of records by the persons to whom the statutory obligation applies. Section 23 regulates the issuance of tax invoices and requires a registered person making a taxable supply to issue a serially numbered tax invoice containing the prescribed particulars, including the name, address and registration number of the supplier and the recipient, as applicable. Subsection (2) of Section 23 further provides that no person other than a registered person or a person paying retail tax shall issue an invoice under that section. Similarly, Section 26 requires every registered person to furnish a true and correct electronic return in the prescribed form and manner within the stipulated period.

30. These provisions are interconnected. The issuance of a tax invoice, the recording of taxable transactions and the filing of electronic returns are integral components of the VAT mechanism. They enable the department to identify the supplier and recipient, verify the transactions, determine output tax and examine the admissibility of input tax. An unregistered person, who has not been allocated a registration number under section 2(24) and has not been brought within the prescribed electronic registration mechanism, cannot ordinarily discharge the statutory obligations in the same manner as a person who has actually been registered. The absence of a statutory mechanism for such a person to issue a tax invoice and file electronic returns in the prescribed manner is a relevant consideration while interpreting the charging provision.

31. The respondent-registered person's failure, if established, to obtain registration despite being legally obliged to do so may attract the consequences specifically provided in terms of section STR No.40130/2022 18 33(7) under the Act. However, the department must distinguish between proceedings for failure to obtain registration and proceedings for determination and recovery of sales tax. The existence of one statutory default does not automatically dispense with the procedure prescribed for the other. The law does not permit the department to substitute an assumed registration for the compulsory registration contemplated by Rule 6 and thereafter impose every consequence of registered status for a period during which the prescribed process had not been completed.

32. An important aspect of the controversy relates to the historical development of the provisions governing compulsory registration. Before the omission of Section 19 of the Act through the Finance Act, 2004, the statute contained an express provision governing compulsory registration and providing for the consequences of such registration, including the deemed date of registration from the day he became liable for registration where the statutory conditions were satisfied.

33. The omission of the aforesaid provision and the subsequent regulation of compulsory registration through the Rules are relevant legislative developments. Under the present framework, Rule 6 prescribes the procedure for compulsory registration and expressly provides under sub-rule (4) that a person compulsorily registered is required to comply with the provisions of the Act and the Rules from the date of compulsory registration. The applicantdepartment has not demonstrated any provision in the applicable statutory framework which permits it to disregard the express language of Rule 6(4) and retrospectively treat the date of compulsory registration as the date on which the person first became liable to obtain registration.

34. It is a settled principle of statutory interpretation that an amendment or omission in the law must be given its proper legal effect. Where the legislature has altered the statutory framework, STR No.40130/2022 19 the Court cannot proceed as though the omitted provision continues to form part of the enactment. In Commissioner of Income Tax v. Lahore Cantonment Cooperative Housing Society (2009 PTD 799), the importance of construing statutory amendments in accordance with their legal effect was recognised. Similarly, the principles discussed in Dad Muhammad and another v. Additional District Judge-I, Quetta and others (1996 SCMR 1688), and Federation of Pakistan v. M/s. Norri Trading Corporation (Pvt.) Ltd. (PTCL 1992 CL 363 (SC)), may be kept in view while examining the consequences flowing from legislative amendment and omission.

35. We are not inclined to attribute to the legislature an intention which is not borne out by the language of the enacted provisions. Nor can an earlier statutory arrangement be imported into the present framework merely because the department considers it more conducive to revenue collection. The obligation to obtain registration and the consequences of failure to obtain it must be determined under the law applicable to the relevant tax periods. The omission of the former provision cannot be ignored while construing the present procedure for compulsory registration.

36. It is an established principle that a fiscal liability must be founded upon clear statutory authority. The charging provision must be construed according to its express language, and neither the department nor the Court can enlarge the scope of a tax by implication. In M/s. Al-Technique Corporation (supra) the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan reiterated the importance of applying the language of the taxing statute in determining the existence and extent of fiscal liability. However, strict construction does not mean that a provision must be interpreted in isolation or that the taxpayer is entitled to defeat an otherwise lawful tax liability by relying upon a technical omission. The Court must ascertain the true meaning of the enactment by reading the STR No.40130/2022 20 charging provision, definitions and machinery provisions together. Reliance is placed on on Messrs Kassim Textile Mills (Pvt.) Limited v. Commissioner Inland Revenue, Karachi (2025 SCMR 1248 ), The Intelligence Officer, Directorate of Intelligence and Investigation, FBR and others v. Abdul Karim and others (2025 SCMR 969) , government of Punjab through Secretary Irrigation and Power and another v. Kunjah Textile Mills Ltd and others (2025 SCMR 239), Federation of Pakistan through Revenue Division and others v. Dewan Motors (Pvt.) Ltd., and others (PLD 2025 SC 394), Commissioner Inland Revenue Zone-IV, Large Taxpayer Unit, Karachi v. Messrs Al-Abid Silk Mills Ltd., A-39, Manghopir Road, Site, Karachi. (2023 SCMR 1797), Commissioner of Income Tax Legal Division, Lahore and others v. Khurshid Ahmad and others (2016 PTD 1393), A&B Food Industries Limited v.Commissioner of Income Tax/Sales, Karachi (1992 PTD 545), B.P. Biscuit Factory Ltd., Karachi v. Wealth tax Officer and another (1996 SCMR 1470), Messrs Mehran Associates Limited v. The Commissioner of Income Tax, Karachi (1993 PTD 69), Commissioner of Income Tax v. Messrs Gilani Transport Company (2017 SCMR 197), Messrs Pakistan Television Corporation Limited v. Commissioner Inland Revenue (Legal), LTU, Islamabad and others (2017 SCMR 1136 ) , Commissioner of Income Tax v. Messrs Eli Lilly Pakistan (Pvt.) Ltd. (2009 PTD 1392), Chairman, Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Bahawalpur and another v. Rizwan Rashid and 3 others (2005 SCMR 728), Commissioner of Agricultural Income-Tax, East Bengal v. B.W.M. Abdur Rahman (1989 PTD 909), The Commissioner of Agricultural Income Tax, East Bengal v. B.W.M. Abdur Rahman, Manager, Taki Bara Taraf Wards Estate (1973 SCMR 445), Muhammadi Steamship Co. Ltd., v. the Commissioner of Income Tax (Central), Karachi (1966 PTD 664) and Messrs Hashwani Botels Limited through Executive Director STR No.40130/2022 21 v. Government of Pakistan through Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Islamabad and 5 others (2004 PTD 901).

37. Another important indication of the legislative intention is available from Section 38 of the Act, which deals with the powers of authorized officers to have access to premises, stocks, accounts and records. The provision separately refers to a registered person and a person liable for registration, among other categories of persons falling within its scope. This distinction is significant. Where the legislature intended to confer powers upon the department in respect of a person who was liable to be registered but had not actually been registered, it expressly employed separate language to that effect.

38. Had the expression "registered person" been intended to include, for every purpose and in every context, a person merely liable to be registered, there would have been little necessity for the legislature to separately identify such category in Section 38. The express distinction demonstrates that the legislature was conscious of the difference between actual registration and liability to obtain registration. It also reinforces the principle that the extended definition contained in Section 2(25) cannot be applied without considering the particular provision in which it occurs.

39. Section 11 of the Act provides the mechanism for assessment and recovery of tax not levied or short-levied or erroneously refunded, subject to the conditions and procedure prescribed therein. The existence of the power of assessment under Section 11 does not confer an unrestricted authority upon the department to create a liability irrespective of the statutory conditions governing the underlying charge. The assessment machinery is intended to quantify and recover a liability which is otherwise legally attracted under the Act. It cannot be treated as an independent charging provision or employed to overcome the STR No.40130/2022 22 limitations arising from the statutory framework governing registration.

40. In other words, the power to assess and recover tax must necessarily be preceded by the existence of a lawful liability and exercised in accordance with the prescribed procedure. The department cannot rely upon Section 11 of the Act to dispense with the requirements of Section 14 and Rule 6 or to assume a status of registration retrospectively without lawful authority.

41. The department's allegation that the respondent-registered person made taxable supplies without obtaining registration must also be examined in the context of Section 2(37), which defines tax fraud, and Section 33, which provides for offences and penalties. The mere fact that a person was liable to obtain registration but failed to do so does not, by itself, establish every ingredient of tax fraud. The department is required to bring the alleged conduct within the particular statutory provision invoked against the taxpayer and establish the relevant ingredients in accordance with law.

42. Likewise, where a person fails to apply for registration despite being legally obliged to do so, the Act provides specific consequences for such default. The department is not rendered powerless merely because the person was not registered during the relevant period. However, the existence of such penal consequences cannot be used as a substitute for the statutory procedure governing compulsory registration and assessment. Each proceeding must stand on its own legal foundation. The department must establish the factual and legal basis of the charge, afford the prescribed opportunity of hearing and determine the liability in accordance with the relevant provisions.

43. In the present matter, the learned Tribunal examined the legality of the demands raised against the respondent-registered person and concluded that the department had not lawfully STR No.40130/2022 23 established its authority to impose sales tax for the periods preceding compulsory registration. Such determination involved interpretation of the relevant statutory provisions and fell within the appellate jurisdiction of the learned Tribunal.

44. In the present controversy, the combined reading of Section 2(24), Section 2(25), Section 3, Section 14, omitted section 19 and Rule 6(4) does not support the proposition that the department may dispense with the compulsory registration procedure and impose the entire liability of a registered person retrospectively for a period preceding the date of such registration.

45. We now advert to the principal authority cited by the applicant-department, namely, S.K. Steel Casting, (Supra). A perusal of the aforesaid judgment reveals that this Court had occasion to examine substantially the same controversy concerning the recovery of sales tax from persons who were liable to be registered but had not actually obtained registration. The questions considered therein included the interpretation of Sections 2(24), 2(25), 3, 6, 14, 22, 23 and 26 of the Act, read with the relevant provisions of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

46. While examining the controversy, this Court considered the statutory mechanism governing the collection and payment of sales tax, including the provisions relating to input tax, output tax, tax invoices, maintenance of records and filing of electronic returns. The Court observed that the definition of registered person contained in Sections 2(24) and 2(25) and the charging provision under Section 3 were required to be read harmoniously with the remaining provisions of the Act. It was further observed that the VAT mechanism contemplated the adjustment of input tax against output tax and the payment of the resultant net liability through the prescribed electronic return. The Court also considered the significance of Section 23, which regulates the issuance of tax invoices, and Section 26, which requires registered persons to STR No.40130/2022 24 furnish electronic returns in the prescribed manner. It was observed that the statutory framework did not provide an unregistered person with the same mechanism for issuance of tax invoices and filing of electronic returns as was available to an actually registered person. While considering Rule 6 of the Rules, this Court emphasized that where the department formed the opinion that a person was liable to be registered, it was required to initiate the prescribed process of compulsory registration. The person concerned was entitled to be confronted with the material forming the basis of the proposed action and afforded an opportunity to contest his liability to registration.

47. The Court further held that, after the person had been registered in accordance with law, the department could proceed to determine his liability under the Act by following the prescribed procedure and affording the necessary opportunity of hearing. The concluding observations contained in paragraph 17 of the aforesaid judgment are particularly relevant and are reproduced below:

“17. In view of the above, our answer to the proposed questions is that the combined reading of the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder manifestly disclose the intention of the law maker that, where a person is liable to be registered, the applicant- department is first required to register that person compulsorily or otherwise in accordance with law, and then charge sales tax from it under Section 3 of the Act and may proceed against that person regarding prior to registration contravention of the provisions of the Act of 1990, if any. In that eventuality, taxpayer shall be entitled to raise all factual and legal objections against the proceedings so initiated or to be initiated by the applicantdepartment which are not dealt with in this judgment.” (emphasis supplied)

A perusal of the above noted para goes to reveal that if the applicant-department initiates or continues proceedings against the taxpayer/registered person, the taxpayer/registered person shall STR No.40130/2022 25 remain at liberty to raise all available factual and legal objections before the competent forum, notwithstanding the observations made in the judgment. The judgment shall not be construed as prejudicing or foreclosing any such objections which have not been specifically adjudicated upon by the Court.

48. It is, therefore, not possible to accept the submission that the learned Tribunal ignored the ratio decidendi of the aforesaid judgment. Rather, the approach adopted by the learned Tribunal is consistent with the principle enunciated therein. The observation in S.K. Steel Casting (supra) that the department may proceed against a taxpayer for pre-registration contraventions is equally important. It prevents a person from claiming complete immunity merely because compulsory registration was effected at a later stage. However, such proceedings must be founded upon the relevant provisions of the Act and cannot be converted into an unrestricted power to impose a retrospective tax demand without satisfying the statutory requirements.

49. The applicant-department has not been able to point out any subsequent statutory amendment applicable to the relevant tax periods or any binding judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan which displaces the aforesaid declaration of law. Consequently, the principle laid down in S.K. Steel Casting (supra) continues to govern the controversy before us.

50. The existence of information suggesting that a person was liable to registration may provide a lawful basis for initiating proceedings for compulsory registration. Such information, however, does not dispense with the requirement of determining the person's liability to registration in accordance with the prescribed procedure. The applicant-department was required to demonstrate that the respondent-registered person had been proceeded against in accordance with Section 14 and Rule 6 of the Rules and that the statutory requirements governing compulsory STR No.40130/2022 26 registration had been satisfied. Thereafter, the department could determine the tax liability, if any, in accordance with the provisions of the Act and by affording the respondent-registered person an effective opportunity of hearing.

51. The appropriate course available to the department was to initiate compulsory registration proceedings, determine the liability of the respondent-registered person in accordance with Rule 6 of the Rules, and thereafter proceed under the relevant provisions of the Act.

52. It is also pertinent to observe that the liability to pay tax and the liability to obtain registration are legally distinct, although interrelated, obligations. The failure to obtain registration may attract consequences under the Act; however, it cannot be presumed that every consequence attached to an actually registered person automatically operates retrospectively from the date on which the person first became liable to registration.

53. Such an interpretation would effectively render the words "from the date of compulsory registration" occurring in Rule 6(4) and scheme of the Act redundant and would defeat the procedure expressly prescribed for determining the status of a person who has failed to obtain registration. We are, therefore, of the considered view that the learned Tribunal has correctly appreciated the distinction between a person actually registered and a person merely liable to be registered, and has rightly concluded that the department could not, in the circumstances of the present case, determine sales tax liability for the preregistration period, particularly in view of the omission of section 19 through Finance Act, 2004, by simply invoking the extended definition contained in Section 2(25) of the Act. The legislative intent underlying the omission of Section 19 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, through the Finance Act, 2004, and the subsequent insertion of sub-rule (4) of Rule 6 Rules, is discernible from the change in STR No.40130/2022 27 the statutory scheme. Whereas the erstwhile Section 19 contemplated deemed registration retrospectively from the date on which a person became liable to be registered, Rule 6(4) expressly requires compliance with the provisions of the Act and the Rules from the date of compulsory registration. This legislative change signifies that the liability arising from compulsory registration is not to be extended retrospectively to the pre-registration period, an interpretation which is also consistent with the scheme and underlying principles of Value Added Tax (VAT).

54. For what has been discussed above, we are of the considered view that the extended definition of "registered person" contained in Section 2(25) of the Act cannot be interpreted in isolation or applied in disregard of the statutory framework governing registration, assessment and payment of sales tax. The expression "liable to be registered" identifies a person upon whom the law imposes an obligation to obtain registration; however, the consequences flowing from actual or compulsory registration must be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder.

55. The combined reading of Sections 2(24),2(25), 3, 6, 7, 11 14 and omitted section 19 of the Act, read with Rule 6 of the Rules, makes it evident that the department is required to follow the prescribed procedure for compulsory registration before proceeding to charge sales tax under Section 3. Rule 6(4), in particular, expressly requires a person compulsorily registered to comply with the provisions of the Act and the Rules from the date of compulsory registration. Such a statutory prescription cannot be rendered ineffective by resorting to an expansive interpretation of the definition clause.

56. The applicant-department has failed to demonstrate that the learned Tribunal committed any error of law in applying the aforesaid principle to the facts and circumstances of the present STR No.40130/2022 28 case. Rather, the impugned order reflects a correct appreciation of the statutory scheme and the distinction between the obligation to obtain registration and the liability to discharge sales tax through the mechanism prescribed for registered persons.

57. Consequently, we find no legal infirmity in the impugned orders dated 15.03.2022 passed by the learned Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Division Bench-I, Islamabad, warranting interference by this Court in its reference jurisdiction, therefore, instant Sales Tax Reference Application, along with connected STR Nos.40131/2022, 40132/2022 and 40134/2022, are dismissed. The impugned orders dated 15.03.2022 passed by the learned Tribunal are maintained.

58. The Office shall transmit a copy of this judgment, duly authenticated under the seal of this Court, to the learned Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Division Bench-1, Islamabad in accordance with law.
